web_evidence.title: Across the River and Into the Trees, by Ernest Hemingway
web_evidence.note: The complete searchable novel predominantly narrates Cantwell externally as he or the Colonel. Chapter XXXV becomes a sustained, unquoted first-person war recollection using I and we, and Chapter XXXVI returns to third-person narration.

web_evidence.title: Ernest Hemingway's Across the River and into the Trees: A Study in Narrative Technique
web_evidence.note: This scholarly study distinguishes the limited heterodiegetic narrator from Cantwell as fixed internal focalizer and describes the third-person duck-shoot frame and extended interior-monologue structure, corroborating the novel's mixed narrative modes.

web_evidence.title: Across the River and into the Trees Chapters 28-36
web_evidence.note: The chapter analysis explicitly states that Chapter 35 switches into a first-person account of Cantwell's past without the filter of the third-person narrator, before the following chapter returns to the present scene.

person_note: The controlling narrative is predominantly a nonparticipating third-person voice closely focalized through Colonel Cantwell. Chapter XXXV contains a single chapter-length first-person interior war account, but it remains subordinate to and embedded within the otherwise third-person novel rather than forming a co-controlling base strand. Under the clarified base-narration rule, the book label is THIRD.
